![](images/9d/9d24a5f692535453b1b34c2bc9236bd44cd2c88c05724a2a5dbdf804b98957e5.svg)

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ is $\mathbf n = \dfrac x2\,\mathbf i + \dfrac y2\,\mathbf j.$*" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179646 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e4ef9955-c544-5a0b-9748-af661e7750b3" "question-7f447fce-ea84-5549-9b80-d5d43d163662"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179647 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ab737fa4-bfd8-53e2-9695-4ad4cbdcb6c6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-765f030b-c4cb-527c-8c26-c947b0ace6a4" :question/id #uuid "765f030b-c4cb-527c-8c26-c947b0ace6a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-127028" :question/problem "![](images/0f/0f1d25942ae680c068b587f38bfbc968c8850b8fa2db2003e994e1ec32dad892.png)

Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the clockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero
- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive
- The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is negative" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Note that the flux $F$ that flows in through $C$ is the same that flows out through $C.$ Therefore, there is no net flow of $F$ through $C.$

![](images/b7/b7acc3028de66ae71ae4e425da639e51a357a77f2b0a345290592cac91ba17d3.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/04/04639a0074aa4607fa57bfe589aad1780f8da6f573d8589a68c2fdb569b5a129.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-406f40cf-3f8f-59a9-9607-1816ee0ec44b"] :db/ensure $$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-4x\,i-4y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-4{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =-4(1-(-1)) \\  & =(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/1d/1de4c4c55784b4a84a0493a4cc65082c430cadcc39c3d808001b2fd27665e968.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(4x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot 2 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=8.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(4x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-3{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =(-3)\cdot 2 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=-6.
$$

Finally, then

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

 

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179866 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the clockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero
- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive
- The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is negative" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Note that the flux $F$ that flows in through $C$ is the same that flows out through $C.$ Therefore, there is no net flow of $F$ through $C.$

![](images/b7/b7acc3028de66ae71ae4e425da639e51a357a77f2b0a345290592cac91ba17d3.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/04/04639a0074aa4607fa57bfe589aad1780f8da6f573d8589a68c2fdb569b5a129.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-406f40cf-3f8f-59a9-9607-1816ee0ec44b"] :db/ensure Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive
- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero
- The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. From the diagram below it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](images/fb/fbcd6fd0fadcc955212a145de9edb4654ddb92ddebb8ba31eb775cff676efeeb.png)

Therefore, the flux is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

- Statement III is true. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/a3/a3d398d382e6bc94ddde77e650d50a6b5ec050083f89f64104f6f2fd172a9239.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177855 :answer-field/correct 17592186177859 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-07e888b6-1046-5ef1-87ef-0610d3939941" :question/id #uuid "07e888b6-1046-5ef1-87ef-0610d3939941" :question/math-academy-id "q-127058" :question/problem "![](images/65/653699a9c78577272425de7f8e6d015743e2c2e8c6e9a21bef189dc06fd80684.png)

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/eb/ebe05a522f9f46acfed63e29927b46f41d78483b5df5e7a15a15ae5f33abd2f4.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-4x\,i-4y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-4{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =-4(1-(-1)) \\  & =(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides ${C}_{2},{C}_{3},$ and ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=4\cdot (-8)=-32.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e89aabf0-d356-583a-a3cf-404273cddd70"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e89aabf0-d356-583a-a3cf-404273cddd70" :answer-field/id #uuid "e89aabf0-d356-583a-a3cf-404273cddd70" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c4eec9b3-71ac-57f5-835f-95347213cc06" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b1bbaa21-1588-571b-867f-6c07807e4cff" "answer-76a9acd9-336e-553e-ac03-9d29b38dee70" "answer-c4eec9b3-71ac-57f5-835f-95347213cc06" "answer-754059dd-7704-537c-8f5b-83a69628877d" "answer-d5afc158-099d-5fca-ba5b-ba5702d29c54"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b1bbaa21-1588-571b-867f-6c07807e4cff" :answer/id #uuid "b1bbaa21-1588-571b-867f-6c07807e4cff" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-76a9acd9-336e-553e-ac03-9d29b38dee70" :answer/id #uuid "76a9acd9-336e-553e-ac03-9d29b38dee70" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-28" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c4eec9b3-71ac-57f5-835f-95347213cc06" :answer/id #uuid "c4eec9b3-71ac-57f5-835f-95347213cc06" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-32" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-754059dd-7704-537c-8f5b-83a69628877d" :answer/id #uuid "754059dd-7704-537c-8f5b-83a69628877d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-64" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d5afc158-099d-5fca-ba5b-ba5702d29c54" :answer/id #uuid "d5afc158-099d-5fca-ba5b-ba5702d29c54" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7f447fce-ea84-5549-9b80-d5d43d163662" :question/id #uuid "7f447fce-ea84-5549-9b80-d5d43d163662" :question/math-academy-id "q-226132" :question/problem "![](images/f4/f413fd04759cdb02118b320fea2f678712681a57f5b08e1bcb57a6843c0c80f0.png)

Consider the vector field $F=4x\,i-3y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/1d/1de4c4c55784b4a84a0493a4cc65082c430cadcc39c3d808001b2fd27665e968.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(4x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot 2 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=8.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(4x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-3{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =(-3)\cdot 2 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=-6.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 8+2\cdot (-6)=4.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a01086e0-9b32-569e-ab08-30e8248e546d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a01086e0-9b32-569e-ab08-30e8248e546d" :answer-field/id #uuid "a01086e0-9b32-569e-ab08-30e8248e546d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-57aeb9a4-34ac-5fdf-99f7-f349f66e9ca1" :answer-field/choices ["answer-10472c8b-0f2c-541f-a4f7-87022439fc30" "answer-83ba3fd3-59b5-593e-9d3a-53cc62cc9e50" "answer-57aeb9a4-34ac-5fdf-99f7-f349f66e9ca1" "answer-8fa05c49-f0b6-5d89-a641-050254ac8771" "answer-721de4ee-1215-587c-a230-6395ae1c468d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-10472c8b-0f2c-541f-a4f7-87022439fc30" :answer/id #uuid "10472c8b-0f2c-541f-a4f7-87022439fc30" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-83ba3fd3-59b5-593e-9d3a-53cc62cc9e50" :answer/id #uuid "83ba3fd3-59b5-593e-9d3a-53cc62cc9e50" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-57aeb9a4-34ac-5fdf-99f7-f349f66e9ca1" :answer/id #uuid "57aeb9a4-34ac-5fdf-99f7-f349f66e9ca1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8fa05c49-f0b6-5d89-a641-050254ac8771" :answer/id #uuid "8fa05c49-f0b6-5d89-a641-050254ac8771" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-721de4ee-1215-587c-a230-6395ae1c468d" :answer/id #uuid "721de4ee-1215-587c-a230-6395ae1c468d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

 

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179866 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186179483 :question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = 8y\,\mathbf i + 4x\,\mathbf j$ and the circle $C$ given by $x^2+y^2 = 4.$ If the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by  

![](images/9d/9d24a5f692535453b1b34c2bc9236bd44cd2c88c05724a2a5dbdf804b98957e5.svg)

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: The outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ is $\mathbf n = \dfrac x2\,\mathbf i + \dfrac y2\,\mathbf j.$*"] ["question-765f030b-c4cb-527c-8c26-c947b0ace6a4" :question/id #uuid "765f030b-c4cb-527c-8c26-c947b0ace6a4"] ["question-765f030b-c4cb-527c-8c26-c947b0ace6a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-127028"] ["question-765f030b-c4cb-527c-8c26-c947b0ace6a4" :question/problem "![](images/0f/0f1d25942ae680c068b587f38bfbc968c8850b8fa2db2003e994e1ec32dad892.png)

Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the clockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero
- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive
- The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is negative"] ["question-765f030b-c4cb-527c-8c26-c947b0ace6a4" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is true, while statement II is false. Note that the flux $F$ that flows in through $C$ is the same that flows out through $C.$ Therefore, there is no net flow of $F$ through $C.$

![](images/b7/b7acc3028de66ae71ae4e425da639e51a357a77f2b0a345290592cac91ba17d3.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/04/04639a0074aa4607fa57bfe589aad1780f8da6f573d8589a68c2fdb569b5a129.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""] ["question-765f030b-c4cb-527c-8c26-c947b0ace6a4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-406f40cf-3f8f-59a9-9607-1816ee0ec44b" "![](images/af/afaec113101f1a63134d2b1cb5c9744b93f9b84dabafaa205780d2dc5b49a7bc.png)

Consider the ellipse $S$ and vector field $F$ shown above. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the clockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is zero
- The flux of $F$ across $C$ is positive
- The flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive"] ["question-1e18756f-1e50-5f09-be71-26f001c4f68e" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero then the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. From the diagram below it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](images/6b/6b24ece279cc480f20d7a4dbc65f7a5257af71f22688b1416c73e3b40673a321.png)

Therefore, the flux is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

- Statement III is true. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/9e/9e8527d26f0f2bd5372d8643f8f9321ec022bb0079e1fc5b23be4978f436613c.png)

So, the flux of $F$ across $-C$ is positive, and we must have

$$
{∮}_{-C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s>0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-1e18756f-1e50-5f09-be71-26f001c4f68e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

In our case, we need to find an expression for the flux across only the part ${C}_{2}$ of the closed curve $C.$ Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have $n=j.$ 

![](images/5d/5d0e9699f75e1f3f727c5c771fdce1a66311496cb55d31c0aac789901feed0cb.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}((x+y)^{2}\,i+(x-y)^{2}\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(x-y)^{2}\,\text{d}s\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/eb/ebe05a522f9f46acfed63e29927b46f41d78483b5df5e7a15a15ae5f33abd2f4.png)

First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-4x\,i-4y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=\,i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-4{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =-4(1-(-1)) \\  & =(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides ${C}_{2},{C}_{3},$ and ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=4\cdot (-8)=-32.
$$"] ["question-e4ef9955-c544-5a0b-9748-af661e7750b3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e89aabf0-d356-583a-a3cf-404273cddd70" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-ab737fa4-bfd8-53e2-9695-4ad4cbdcb6c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-226136"] ["question-ab737fa4-bfd8-53e2-9695-4ad4cbdcb6c6" :question/problem "![](images/9d/9da6bdb9ab5f93d0b0d11dfd60ab2b647380a94ce337c2314ec3504cabafa889.png)

Consider the vector field $F=4x\,i-3y\,j$ and a square $C$ with side length $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*"] ["question-ab737fa4-bfd8-53e2-9695-4ad4cbdcb6c6" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/1d/1de4c4c55784b4a84a0493a4cc65082c430cadcc39c3d808001b2fd27665e968.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(4x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot 2 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=8.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(4x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-3{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =(-3)\cdot 2 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=-6.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 8+2\cdot (-6)=4.
$$"] ["question-ab737fa4-bfd8-53e2-9695-4ad4cbdcb6c6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-a01086e0-9b32-569e-ab08-30e8248e546d" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-ab737fa4-bfd8-53e2-9695-4ad4cbdcb6c6"] [17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

 

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$"] [17592186179866 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0]] "retractions" [[17592186179483 :question/problem "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = 8y\,\mathbf i + 4x\,\mathbf j$ and the circle $C$ given by $x^2+y^2 = 4.$ If the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

:question/problem "Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf F$ shown below. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

Which of the following statements are true?

- The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is negative

- The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is zero

- The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is positive

![](images/7e/7e7fbe6aaf1310b186344a3cf5a127075f11a86b51db2e687ddc7035d5d890f8.png)" :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C\mathbin:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

The outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. From the diagram below we see that $\mathbf F$ acts perpendicular to $\mathbf n$ at every point on $C.$ Therefore, there is no net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

![](images/4a/4a3d9864bb6bada1fd218b299427bc5bb4ffcbcccb1a504fff77416d5d292151.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

- Statement III is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/93/9310d17389f61de2984c0e23cfe1060e77d4a87a140d2f1c892bdbab9b99629b.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
\oint\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186049212} {:db/id 17592186049653} {:db/id 17592186050104} {:db/id 17592186180031 :question/id #uuid "a2d693ae-0e11-561b-9b69-4ee74bfcc078" :question/math-academy-id "q-126726" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186179644 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2b7b8782-d1f4-5654-a18f-6ad35de8fb30" :knowledge-point/title "Determining a Flux's Sign From a Diagram"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10859d25-668f-5816-af25-2f8f651c2adc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186177856} {:answer/id #uuid "25ee1056-9705-59ee-9a75-4c87721c080a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186177857} {:answer/id #uuid "3ca5ffeb-70c8-5dd6-ad43-d4b589b2f907" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186177858} {:answer/id #uuid "51f614c5-97b9-5cf0-9215-eafa949f0a67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186177859} {:answer/id #uuid "67764856-b008-565b-9f53-6d0005aa71c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186177860}] :answer-field/id #uuid "45251c46-c4eb-5ef4-a338-46c73974a207" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186177855}] :question/problem "![](images/e6/e679efaa2612d45bbfe8b918de7148853b64eaf530af34a525ef1735e0946b09.png)

:knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186179646 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "349c29ae-5eb5-5454-a98f-c1adac3d7108" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Flux Across a Square Using Symmetry"}] :question/problem "![](images/05/05c91d681a0c84bbe9d8b6cab9bd8cdf1dca8bf88c851b8c7a7045f73ff9844c.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F = 2x\,\mathbf i + 2y\,\mathbf j$ and a square $C$ with side length $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across all four sides of the square.*" :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/1d/1de4c4c55784b4a84a0493a4cc65082c430cadcc39c3d808001b2fd27665e968.png)

First, consider the side $C_1.$ We have that $\mathbf n_1 = \mathbf i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(2x\,i+2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \mathbf i + t\,\mathbf j, \quad \Rightarrow\quad \mathbf r'(t) = \mathbf j, \qquad t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =2(1-(-1)) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integrals over the sides $C_2, C_3,$ and $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 4\cdot 4 = 16.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048512} {:db/id 17592186180036 :question/id #uuid "ea876586-e09c-5050-847d-bc8b312ea302" :question/math-academy-id "q-126881"} {:db/id 17592186180042 :question/id #uuid Two Symmetry Properties"}] :question/problem "![](images/59/59b5f1676f036f80e6aa2e9e331327ed9ec28e88bacda52a91ee0865736e9ce3.png)

Consider the vector field $\mathbf F = 5x\,\mathbf i - 3y\,\mathbf j$ and a rectangle $C$ with base $4$ and height $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$ 

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*" :question/worked-solution "If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/79/793755cda5243dbb427d8722c21ab150a4821c3957f0ccd0ef0fedbbd576e924.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side $C_1.$ We have that $\mathbf n_1 = \mathbf i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(5x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =5{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_1,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = 2\mathbf i + t\,\mathbf j, \quad \Rightarrow\quad \mathbf r'(t) = \mathbf j, \qquad t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =5{\int }_{-1}^{1}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =10{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =10\cdot 2 \\  & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_3$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s = 20.
$$

- Next, we consider the side $C_2.$ We have that $\mathbf n_2 = \mathbf j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(5x\,i-3y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side $C_2,$ we have

$$
\mathbf r(t) = t\,\mathbf i + \mathbf j, \quad \Rightarrow\quad \mathbf r'(t) = \mathbf i, \qquad t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-3{\int }_{-2}^{2}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =(-3)\cdot 4 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side $C_4$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = -12.
$$

Finally, then

$$
\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s= 2 \cdot 20 + 2 \cdot (-12) = 16.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180037 :question/id #uuid "2e3c5efb-b46d-57f5-8660-cecbe88198e4" :question/math-academy-id "q-126892"} {:db/id 17592186180043 :question/id #uuid $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. Imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water, and $C$ is a curve that allows water to flow through it (like a fishing net). 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol C$** is a scalar number that tells us how much water is escaping the region bounded by $C.$ 

We have three possible scenarios: 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

![](images/6f/6ff4d006d3fbf4a434f35a13c8591fc166ff6c74adf2b7969752b7541e486df2.png)

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/38/3812148e855a84e3233316acc8bbf59bd7cd802a874c9e4807c6efd7ca6754cf.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

The following vector field has zero flux across $C$ because the amount of water flowing in through $C$ equals the amount of water flowing out through $C.$

![](images/56/56aef4f217e9981755826745a97e8389d86b49518ffd7d3ebc75e5ee2dc28f8b.png)

The following two vector fields also have a zero flux across $C$ because the water flow is tangential to $C$ at every point along $C.$

![](images/63/637677324152af3d428e405c89025f35dbe5d71e2e8f0a0797ef3aca30bae7e1.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ecd8591f-8e5b-50b2-91a1-4f15bd97b2c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9521 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1e80fc64-e097-5e8d-a35c-056416216619" :step/math-academy-id 184955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180342}} {:db/id 17592186180342 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180788 :tutorial/content "If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](images/6d/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

![](images/49/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png)

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

![](images/ac/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png)

Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a328d4d8-bfe8-50eb-8bbd-281b3bb07afe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9522 :tutorial/title "Constructing an Integral Formula for the Flux"} :step/id #uuid "9dac0bb5-3a03-56c0-a614-dc9f045cb3e3" :step/math-academy-id 184956 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180343}} {:db/id 17592186180343 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180789 :tutorial/content "Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf F$ below. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

![](images/e6/e679efaa2612d45bbfe8b918de7148853b64eaf530af34a525ef1735e0946b09.png)

By drawing an outward-pointing unit normal vector, it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](images/fb/fbcd6fd0fadcc955212a145de9edb4654ddb92ddebb8ba31eb775cff676efeeb.png)

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is positive, and we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0.
$$

When measuring flux through a closed curve, the curve's orientation does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same in either case. 

![](images/a3/a3d398d382e6bc94ddde77e650d50a6b5ec050083f89f64104f6f2fd172a9239.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is also positive, and we have

$$
\oint\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "36b855d8-9994-5c22-bbc4-e28065875f84" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9523 :tutorial/title "Orientation-Independence"} :step/id #uuid "a000a04f-fdd8-5b25-9b23-e59a14a3592d" :step/math-academy-id 184957 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180344}} {:db/id 17592186180344 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179644 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179482 :question/id #uuid "c427d9b4-2944-5edc-8e19-363de348d23d" :question/math-academy-id "e-15147"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2b7b8782-d1f4-5654-a18f-6ad35de8fb30" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049212} {:db/id 17592186049653} {:db/id 17592186050104}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180031} {:db/id 17592186180032} {:db/id 17592186262687} {:db/id 17592186262688} {:db/id 17592186262690} {:db/id 17592186262691}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining a Flux's Sign From a Diagram"} :step/id #uuid "4f8760a0-8c8e-5ec6-9492-0ecc32789da6" :step/math-academy-id 184958 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180345}} {:db/id 17592186180345 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "472c362c-27a5-5041-90c3-4533c63b736d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9524 :tutorial/title "Calculating Flux"} :step/id #uuid "ab771459-c3a6-5f4b-9e75-cfa3f13b9add" :step/math-academy-id 184961 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180346}} {:db/id 17592186180346 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179645 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179483 :question/id #uuid "15426c37-1508-5407-ab49-b26f8761795c" :question/math-academy-id "e-15148"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9c8ca56-5ea8-547c-80ab-6b1f1347447e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180034} {:db/id 17592186180035} {:db/id 17592186235531} {:db/id 17592186262697} {:db/id 17592186262698} {:db/id 17592186262699} {:db/id 17592186262700} {:db/id 17592186262701} {:db/id 17592186362496}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Integral Expression for Flux"} :step/id #uuid "2c288a88-997c-5ef1-98ff-24092e7506f9" :step/math-academy-id 184962 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180347}} {:db/id 17592186180347 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180791 :tutorial/content "Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry.

To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

![](images/8e/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png)

If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/65/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png)

Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

This is easy to verify, since, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ 

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
=
-\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53e768e4-a3bb-5b89-83b9-a97e9ff4a921" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9525 :tutorial/title "Using  Symmetry to Simplify Flux Calculations"} :step/id #uuid $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a328d4d8-bfe8-50eb-8bbd-281b3bb07afe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9522 :tutorial/title "Constructing an Integral Formula for the Flux"} :step/id #uuid "9dac0bb5-3a03-56c0-a614-dc9f045cb3e3" :step/math-academy-id 184956 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180343}} {:db/id 17592186180788 :tutorial/content "If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](images/6d/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

![](images/49/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png)

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

![](images/ac/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png)

Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a328d4d8-bfe8-50eb-8bbd-281b3bb07afe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9522 :tutorial/title "Constructing an Integral Formula for the Flux"} {:db/id 17592186180343 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180789 :tutorial/content "Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf F$ below. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

![](images/e6/e679efaa2612d45bbfe8b918de7148853b64eaf530af34a525ef1735e0946b09.png)

By drawing an outward-pointing unit normal vector, it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](images/fb/fbcd6fd0fadcc955212a145de9edb4654ddb92ddebb8ba31eb775cff676efeeb.png)

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is positive, and we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0.
$$

When measuring flux through a closed curve, the curve's orientation does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same in either case. 

![](images/a3/a3d398d382e6bc94ddde77e650d50a6b5ec050083f89f64104f6f2fd172a9239.png)

$$

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "472c362c-27a5-5041-90c3-4533c63b736d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9524 :tutorial/title "Calculating Flux"} :step/id #uuid "ab771459-c3a6-5f4b-9e75-cfa3f13b9add" :step/math-academy-id 184961 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180346}} {:db/id 17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry.

To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

![](images/8e/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png)

If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/65/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png)

Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

This is easy to verify, since, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ 

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
=
-\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53e768e4-a3bb-5b89-83b9-a97e9ff4a921" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9525 :tutorial/title "Using  Symmetry to Simplify Flux Calculations"} :step/id #uuid "5c82115b-5b07-5765-b4a2-64382478cffb" :step/math-academy-id 184965 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180348}} {:db/id 17592186180791 :tutorial/content "Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. - The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is negative

- The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is zero

- The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is positive

![](images/7e/7e7fbe6aaf1310b186344a3cf5a127075f11a86b51db2e687ddc7035d5d890f8.png)" 17592186045417] [17592186179482 1072 #uuid "c427d9b4-2944-5edc-8e19-363de348d23d" 17592186045417] [17592186179482 1074 "If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by $C\mathbin:$ 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/a7/a72dc9866562a42a49590fd169424307675b2c14b36833bd729026f46b677eec.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

![](images/3a/3a6ac8656b2e0b5cc482a16eb3a4fab57cb681c9a40cf634da47f9a4323d9fdf.png)

The outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. From the diagram below we see that $\mathbf F$ acts perpendicular to $\mathbf n$ at every point on $C.$ Therefore, there is no net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

![](images/4a/4a3d9864bb6bada1fd218b299427bc5bb4ffcbcccb1a504fff77416d5d292151.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

- Statement III is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on $C$ in either case.

![](images/93/9310d17389f61de2984c0e23cfe1060e77d4a87a140d2f1c892bdbab9b99629b.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is zero, and we must have

$$
\oint\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$
